title: Complex numbers as rotations
description: Use complex numbers to represent rotation and connect exponentials to oscillations.
heading: Why does one exponential describe an entire oscillation?
lead: Complex multiplication packages amplitude and phase into a geometric operation that simplifies linear dynamics.
outcomes: Convert between Cartesian and polar forms and divide complex numbers.
Recover a real oscillation from a complex exponential.

blocks.body:
Imagine watching a dot travel uniformly around a circle while a lamp projects its shadow onto a horizontal ruler. The dot never reverses its direction of travel, yet the shadow repeatedly slows, stops and reverses. Circular motion and oscillation are two views of the same geometric construction. We want a notation that keeps the circular motion simple while allowing us to recover the measured shadow.

A pair of real coordinates already locates the dot. Complex numbers add a multiplication rule that makes these pairs especially useful: multiplication can rotate and stretch the plane. The symbol $i$ is defined by $i^2=-1$. This introduces a larger number system in which the ordered pair $(a,b)$ is written $a+ib$, with familiar algebra consistent with that defining rule.

Adding phases, dividing oscillatory responses and differentiating repeated oscillations become compact calculations. A complex representation need not mean that measured displacement is complex. Often the physical observable is explicitly the real part of a complex calculation. Keeping that instruction visible prevents a convenient mathematical representation from becoming a mysterious extra physical dimension.

data.title: Multiplication by i preserves radius
data.caption: 3 + 2i becomes −2 + 3i under a counterclockwise quarter turn. Both radii are √13; the axes use equal scales.

blocks.title: 1. Give pairs a multiplication that rotates
blocks.body:
Write $z=a+ib$, with real numbers $a$ and $b$. Its real part is $\operatorname{Re}z=a$ and its imaginary part is $\operatorname{Im}z=b$; the imaginary part is the real coefficient, not $ib$. On an Argand diagram, a is the horizontal coordinate and b the vertical coordinate. Addition is coordinatewise. Thus addition has the familiar geometry of placing displacements head to tail.

Multiplication follows distribution and $i^2=-1$:
$$(a+ib)(c+id)=(ac-bd)+i(ad+bc).$$
The minus sign is essential. Multiplying $a+ib$ by i gives $-b+ia$, mapping $(a,b)$ to $(-b,a)$. This is a counterclockwise quarter turn. Applying it twice gives $(-a,-b)$, exactly multiplication by −1. The defining algebra therefore has a concrete geometric meaning.

The distance to the origin is the **modulus** $|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. The **complex conjugate** $\overline z=a-ib$ reflects the point across the real axis. Multiplication gives $z\overline z=a^2+b^2=|z|^2$, a real nonnegative number. This identity supplies division: for nonzero z, $1/z=\overline z/|z|^2$. Multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's conjugate; the denominator becomes an ordinary positive real number.

For example, $(1+i)/(1-i)=(1+i)^2/2=i$. Its modulus is one and its direction is vertical. Substitution checks the result: $i(1-i)=1+i$. Zero still has no reciprocal; extending the real numbers has not made division by zero possible. Conjugation distributes over sums and products. Later it will help construct positive lengths in complex vector spaces, where simply squaring components would fail: $i^2$ is negative, while $\overline i\,i=1$.

further.question: Why use a conjugate in division?
further.answer: It turns the denominator into its positive squared modulus.

further.question: Can zero have a reciprocal?
further.answer: No. No product with zero is one.

blocks.title: 2. Polar form makes composition transparent
blocks.body:
For a nonzero point, let $r=|z|$ and let $\theta$ be its counterclockwise angle from the positive real axis, in radians. Circle geometry gives $a=r\cos\theta$ and $b=r\sin\theta$, hence $z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$. This is **polar form**. Adding an integer multiple of $2\pi$ to the angle gives the same point. At the origin no particular angle is selected. An argument of a complex number means a chosen angle representing its direction, with this ambiguity understood.

To recover an angle from Cartesian coordinates, inspect the quadrant as well as the tangent. Both $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$ give $b/a=1$, but their directions differ by $\pi$. A calculator's two-coordinate angle function retains that information. Full-turn ambiguity is harmless for the point, but matters when tracking a continuous phase through several revolutions.

Multiply two polar expressions and use the angle addition identities. The real component becomes $r_1r_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)$ and the imaginary component becomes $r_1r_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)$. Moduli multiply and arguments add. Division divides moduli and subtracts arguments. A complex number is consequently both a point and an instruction to stretch by its modulus and rotate by its argument.

For instance, $1+i$ has modulus $\sqrt2$ and angle $\pi/4$. Squaring doubles the angle and squares the modulus, giving radius 2 at angle $\pi/2$, hence $2i$. Expansion agrees. Roots reverse this reasoning, but angle ambiguity produces multiple answers: the square roots of −1 have angles $\pi/2$ and $3\pi/2$, giving i and −i. Choosing only one loses a solution.

This viewpoint is useful when a device changes the amplitude and phase of a sinusoidal input. Such a change can be encoded by one complex multiplier. Connecting two devices multiplies their factors, so amplitude ratios multiply and phase shifts add. This assumes the model acts linearly on that frequency; arbitrary nonlinear operations do not inherit the rule.

blocks.title: 3. Exponentials describe the rotating dot
blocks.body:
The exponential has the series $e^x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^n/n!$. Define the complex exponential by the same series with complex input. It converges absolutely for every finite complex number, permitting grouping of even and odd terms. Powers of i cycle through $1,i,-1,-i$. Consequently
$$e^{i\theta}=\left(1-\frac{\theta^2}{2!}+\frac{\theta^4}{4!}-\cdots\right)+i\left(\theta-\frac{\theta^3}{3!}+\cdots\right)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta.$$
This is Euler's formula. The two series are the sine and cosine series developed through Taylor expansion. Their convergence here is global. We have compared convergent representations, rather than guessed from notation.

Polar form becomes $z=re^{i\theta}$. Describe the dot by $z(t)=Ae^{i(\omega t+\phi)}$, where A is its nonnegative radius, $\omega$ its angular frequency and $\phi$ its initial phase. Its horizontal projection is $x(t)=\operatorname{Re}z(t)=A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$. The exponent is dimensionless. When t is in seconds, $\omega$ has units of inverse seconds, conventionally called radians per second. For positive angular frequency, one revolution takes $2\pi/\omega$; the ordinary frequency is $\omega/(2\pi)$.

Differentiation with respect to real time acts on the two components separately. It gives $z'=i\omega z$ and $z''=-\omega^2z$. Therefore the shadow satisfies $x''=-\omega^2x$. Multiplication by i explains the quarter-cycle shift between displacement and velocity, and why acceleration points opposite displacement. Two derivatives reveal the oscillator equation without repeatedly expanding trigonometric identities.

A constant complex amplitude C can absorb the initial phase: $x(t)=\operatorname{Re}(Ce^{i\omega t})$. If $C=a+ib$, this is $a\cos\omega t-b\sin\omega t$. The minus sign comes from multiplication. Given initial position $x_0$ and velocity $v_0$, choose $C=x_0-iv_0/\omega$ when $\omega\ne0$. A complex constant stores two real initial numbers.

Taking real parts commutes with real linear operations such as addition, differentiation and multiplication by real coefficients. It does not commute with arbitrary nonlinear operations: $\operatorname{Re}(z^2)$ generally differs from $(\operatorname{Re}z)^2$. This is why the technique works naturally for linear oscillator equations but cannot be applied blindly to a nonlinear force law. The connection between mathematical representation and physical trajectory must remain explicit.

blocks.heading: Why regrouping is legitimate
blocks.body: Absolute convergence means $\sum |(i\theta)^n/n!|$ is finite. The ratio of successive magnitudes is $|\theta|/(n+1)$, eventually below a fixed number less than one, so a geometric tail bounds the sum. Grouping even and odd terms is safe. Such regrouping is not automatically safe for a conditionally convergent series.

blocks.heading: The same rotation written as a number and as a matrix
blocks.body:
Multiply $z=x+iy$ by $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$. Expanding and collecting real and imaginary parts gives
$$x'=x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta,\qquad y'=x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta.$$
These are exactly the entries of a real linear map:
$$\binom{x'}{y'}=
\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\binom{x}{y}.$$
Complex multiplication and a two-dimensional rotation matrix are two representations of the same action.

Multiplication by i corresponds to $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Calculate $J^2=-I$: two quarter-turns reverse every vector. The identity $i^2=-1$ therefore has a direct geometric counterpart. Expanding the matrix exponential in powers of J separates its even and odd powers, giving $e^{\theta J}=I\cos\theta+J\sin\theta$.

For rotation at constant angular speed, $\dot z=i\omega z$ has solution $z(t)=e^{i\omega t}z(0)$. In real coordinates it is the coupled system $\dot x=-\omega y$, $\dot y=\omega x$. Differentiating again gives $\ddot x=-\omega^2x$: the oscillator is one coordinate of a rotating state.

The bridge connects three chapters at once: exponential evolution, linear maps and oscillations. Complex notation earns its usefulness by simplifying a specific real structure. It does not make every pair of real equations into a rotation; the coupling must have the form shown here.

blocks.nextConnection: We next use rate laws and initial data to select a trajectory from a family of possible motions.

data.coreIdea: Complex multiplication packages scaling and rotation, allowing amplitude and phase to be manipulated as one algebraic object. The real and imaginary parts are not competing answers but coordinates of one representation whose modulus and argument carry different information.
data.widerConnection: Complex notation simplifies oscillators, Fourier analysis, contour reasoning, and finite-dimensional quantum models. Its value is structural: multiplication, differentiation, and phase shifts become operations that preserve the relationships we care about.
